title: Negotiation Tactics & Scripts
summary: Concrete phrasing and sequencing for a comp negotiation call: how to anchor, how to counter without a competing offer, and how to stay collaborative while still asking for more.

slides.markdown:
Almost every initial offer has real room in it, because recruiters build in slack for exactly this conversation — companies that intended zero flexibility wouldn't budget for it, and most do. The gap between candidates who leave money on the table and candidates who don't is rarely about leverage; it's about knowing the actual sequence and phrasing of a counter.

This topic covers the concrete mechanics: why a counter is expected rather than adversarial, how to anchor a number without giving away your floor, a script for opening the conversation, and how to negotiate credibly even with no competing offer in hand — while staying collaborative enough that you don't damage the relationship you're about to start working inside.

slides.sectionTitle: Why almost every initial offer has room
slides.markdown:
Recruiters typically start below the top of a level's band, both to leave themselves negotiating room and because most candidates don't counter at all — a surprisingly large share of offers get accepted at the initial number with zero pushback, which is exactly why companies can afford to open low.

This isn't universal: some companies (often larger, process-heavy ones) do issue a genuinely "best and final" first offer, and treating every offer as automatically negotiable can misfire there. But the default assumption should be that a counter is expected and normal, not confrontational — recruiters negotiate comp packages daily and are rarely offended by a reasonable, well-justified ask.

The real risk isn't asking; it's asking without a clear, defensible number, which reads as fishing rather than negotiating.

slides.sectionTitle: Anchoring: giving a number vs. making them go first
slides.markdown:
| | Giving a number/range first | Making the recruiter go first |
|---|---|---|
| Risk | Anchoring too low leaves money on the table; anchoring too high with no justification can read as unrealistic | None directly, but a vague answer ("I'm flexible") often gets read as low expectations |
| When it works well | You have solid market data and real conviction in the number | Early in the process, before you have enough data to anchor confidently |
| Best move | State a **range** anchored near the top of what your research supports, not a single soft number | Redirect: "I'd love to hear the band for this role first, then I can share my expectations" |

In practice, whoever names a credible number first usually anchors the conversation — so once you have real market data, naming a well-justified range near the top of it is usually stronger than deflecting indefinitely. Deflection is a reasonable opening move only while you're still gathering data.

slides.sectionTitle: A script for opening a counter-offer conversation
slides.subTitle: By email
slides.markdown:
```
Subject: Re: Offer for [Role] — quick follow-up

Hi [Recruiter name],

Thank you again for the offer — I'm excited about the team and the
problems described in the loop. I've had a chance to review the full
package and wanted to follow up on comp before I confirm.

Based on my research for this level and location (levels.fyi, my own
network, and the scope discussed in the loop), I was hoping we could get
closer to $X base / $Y equity. I'm flexible on how that's structured —
base, equity, or a sign-on could all work — but wanted to see if there's
room to move closer to that range.

Happy to hop on a call if that's easier to discuss live. Thanks again for
all your help through the process.

[Your name]
```

Note the structure: gratitude first, a specific number backed by named evidence, explicit flexibility on which lever moves, and an open door to discuss live — every part is doing deliberate work, not filler.

slides.sectionTitle: The same script, live on a call
slides.markdown:
The same structure works verbally, but the sequencing matters more live because there's less time to compose. A workable order: thank them, state that you're excited about the role, name your specific ask with the evidence behind it in one breath, then stop talking.

The pause after your ask is doing real work — many candidates fill silence with justification or backpedaling ("but I understand if that's not possible"), which softens the ask before the other side has even responded. Recruiters are trained to sit in silence; candidates usually aren't, and that asymmetry is exactly what erodes an ask that was otherwise well-built.

If they need to check internally (common, and expected), a clean close is: "totally understand — what's a good time for you to follow up?" This keeps momentum without pressuring them into an answer they don't yet have authority to give.

A competing offer is the strongest lever, but its absence doesn't mean you have none. Without one, substitute concrete, specific evidence for the raw leverage a competing number provides:

- **Market data**, cited specifically ("levels.fyi shows the median for this level and location at $X") rather than vaguely ("I've heard offers can be higher").
- **Scope evidence** from your own résumé or the loop itself — a specific project, system, or outcome that maps to the level or band you're asking for.
- **Genuine enthusiasm paired with a real number**, not a bluff — "this is my top choice and I want to make it work, here's what would get me there" reads very differently from a vague ask with no anchor.

Without a competing offer, expect a smaller movement than you'd get with one — but a well-evidenced ask still routinely moves an offer 3-8%, which is real money over several years even without any external leverage.

The tone that works best treats the recruiter as a partner solving a shared problem — "how do we get this to a number that works for both of us" — rather than an adversary to be beaten. This isn't just etiquette; recruiters who like a candidate genuinely advocate harder internally, and a negotiation that damages the relationship can quietly cost you goodwill in your first year.

Concretely: acknowledge constraints when they're stated ("I understand base has less room than equity"), thank them for specific things they've already done, and frame pushback as information-sharing ("here's what I'm seeing in the market") rather than accusation ("this offer is too low").

Collaborative tone and a firm ask aren't in tension — you can say "I need this to be $X" warmly just as easily as coldly, and the warm version tends to get a better internal advocate on the other end of the phone.

slides.sectionTitle: An ultimatum you're not actually willing to enforce
slides.subTitle: Pitfall
slides.markdown:
A common overcorrection from candidates who've read "be firm" advice: issuing a hard ultimatum ("I need $X or I walk") without actually being willing to walk. Recruiters negotiate constantly and can often tell the difference between a genuine walk-away number and a bluff — and if they call it, you're stuck either backing down (which costs you far more credibility than never bluffing at all) or actually walking from an offer you wanted.

The safer version of firmness is a **specific, justified ask** stated plainly, not a threat. "I'd need this to be $X to accept" is firm without being a bluffed ultimatum, provided $X is a number you'd genuinely walk from if refused — if you wouldn't actually walk, don't frame it as a walk-away line.

If you do have a real walk-away number, state it once, clearly, and let it stand — repeating an ultimatum multiple times in the same conversation reads as anxious rather than confident.

Most successful negotiations take one or two rounds, not an open-ended back-and-forth. Round one is your initial counter with evidence; round two, if the first response falls short, is a narrower, more specific ask ("could we meet in the middle at $X") rather than repeating the same pitch.

A third round is unusual and should generally only happen if new information has entered the picture — a competing offer just landed, or the recruiter came back with a genuinely different structure to react to. Continuing to push after two clean rounds with no new information starts to read as not knowing when to stop, which is its own kind of signal to a company you're about to join.

Knowing this cadence in advance also reduces the anxiety of the conversation — you're not guessing how long to keep pushing, you have a rough plan for exactly two exchanges before deciding whether to accept, walk, or ask for time.

slides.sectionTitle: What a staff-level negotiator does differently
slides.markdown:
A junior negotiator asks for a number. A more experienced one negotiates the *shape* of the package to match what they actually value — trading a larger sign-on for less equity if they're skeptical of the stock, or trading base for equity if they believe in the company's upside and want to optimize taxes by taking more of the comp as long-term capital gains eventually.

This works because recruiters often have more flexibility to reshuffle a fixed total between components than to increase the total itself — asking "could we shift $10k from base into equity" is sometimes an easier internal approval than asking for $10k more overall, since it doesn't change the headline total the company reports internally.

Knowing your own risk tolerance and tax situation well enough to make this trade is what separates a merely competent negotiation from one that actually optimizes the outcome for you specifically, not just for the biggest number.

slides.sectionTitle: From a single offer to real leverage
slides.markdown: Everything in this topic assumes you're negotiating one offer largely on its own merits. [Competing offers and leverage](competing-offers-leverage) covers what changes when you actually have two or more offers to work with — sequencing, disclosure, and how much a specific competing number typically moves the needle, which is a meaningfully different and stronger version of this same conversation.
